sections.h2: Which offices touch a Woodbridge property tax bill?
sections.html:
Three public desks shape a Woodbridge bill. One township office decides what each parcel is worth, a second prints the bill and accepts payment, and the county tax board hears owners who disagree with the first. The county's own page notes that the municipality does the collecting and passes the county's portion along afterward.

Woodbridge property tax errands and the office for each, from the township Assessor and Tax Collector pages and the Middlesex Tax Board page
OfficeHandlesAddress, phone, hours
Township Tax AssessorSetting each parcel's value, new construction included, and administering tax appealsMunicipal Building, 1 Main Street, Woodbridge 07095. Phone 732-602-6002
Tax Collection OfficeBilling and payment for property tax and for water and sewerFirst floor of Town Hall, 1 Main Street. Open Monday to Friday from 8:30 a.m., closing at 4:30 p.m. except Tuesday at 6:30 p.m.
Middlesex County Tax BoardCertifying assessments and ruling on appealsCounty Administration Building, 4th floor, New Brunswick 08901. Phone 732-745-3350. Open Monday to Friday, 8:30 a.m. until 4:15 p.m.

The Assessor must hold a state certification, and the township page cites N.J.S.A. 54:1-35.25. The Tax Board serves all 25 municipalities in the county.

sections.h2: What is the Woodbridge billing calendar?
sections.html:
The year splits into four installments, due on February 1, May 1, August 1 and November 1. The township mails its bills twice, in January and July.

Sewer runs on its own track. One notice posted for the second-half sewer bill named October 1 as the due date and Friday, October 10 as the final day before penalty, and it added that the date of receipt counts, not the postmark. Check the stub on your own bill for the dates that apply to you.

If your closing lands near an installment date, phone the Tax Collection Office first and ask what happens to a payment that arrives late.

sections.h2: What are the ways to pay Woodbridge taxes?
sections.html:
Woodbridge accepts payment five ways.

  • Online, through the Taxpayer Information site. Search for your property, choose Make Payment, and follow the prompts. Electronic checks add $1.95, and cards add roughly 2.95 percent.
  • Over the counter in Town Hall, first floor, in cash or by check or money order.
  • In the drop-off box outside Town Hall.
  • By mail, with the check made out to Township of Woodbridge and sent to P.O. Box 5004, Woodbridge, NJ 07095.
  • Through ACH direct withdrawal, using separate forms for tax and sewer.

Tuesday is the late evening at the counter. A seller clearing a balance just ahead of the deed will likely find online payment or a certified check at the window the fastest.

sections.h2: What is the route for contesting a Woodbridge assessment?
sections.html:
Disputes over value are not decided at Town Hall. The county tax board takes petitions through the online portal at my.njappeal.com, where you create a login and can attach evidence up to seven calendar days before your hearing date, with a 4:00 p.m. limit.

Two filing cutoffs matter here. Added or omitted assessments must be physically in the board's hands by 4:15 p.m. on December 1, and a weekend or holiday date moves to the next business day. A homeowner whose senior or disabled deduction was refused files Form A-1 by April 1 after the refusal.

For an everyday assessment appeal, ask the Tax Board at 732-745-3350 which date goes with the notice you received. In added or omitted cases, an appraiser whose report is offered must be present to testify.

sections.h2: Which Woodbridge tax breaks should an owner check?
sections.html:
Qualifying owners aged 65 or older, or disabled, can deduct $250 from the yearly bill once they have lived in New Jersey for a year. Ownership and occupancy on October 1 of the pretax year, a timely application and an income ceiling all apply.

  • Form PTD plus proofs goes to the township assessor or collector.
  • Form PD5 renews the deduction by March 1 each year.
  • A surviving spouse or civil union partner who is 55 or older may keep it on the same home.
  • The township's Tax Collector page carries a veteran deduction form.

A Property Tax Relief filing event took place at the Division of Taxation in Trenton on November 2, 2026, with four regional offices open until 8:00 p.m. It is over, so ask the Division about the next window.

sections.h2: How should a Woodbridge seller handle unpaid tax?
sections.html:
Get a written balance for your block and lot from the Tax Collection Office before the contract is signed. With quarterly billing, a closing in the middle of a quarter can leave part of a period to settle, so ask how a late payment is credited.

Put the receipts for recent quarters in the closing folder. A separate sewer balance needs its own figure, because sewer follows a different calendar, and the buyer's closing agent will want both numbers.

If the assessed value looks wrong, take that up with the Assessor at 732-602-6002 before listing the house.

sections.h2: What should owners know about the Woodbridge area itself?
sections.html:
Woodbridge was chartered by Charles II on June 1, 1669, and ranks as the oldest original township in New Jersey. At 24.61 square miles in northern Middlesex County, it held 103,639 people in 2020, the seventh-largest count among the state's municipalities. The Census Bureau's 2025 estimate is 104,802.

No incorporated towns sit inside it. Instead it is a set of communities: Avenel, Colonia, Fords, Hopelawn, Iselin, Keasbey, Menlo Park Terrace, Port Reading, Sewaren and Woodbridge proper, each with its own ZIP code or census place. A mayor and a nine-member council run the government under the Faulkner Act.

Transportation is the area's calling card. Turnpike Exit 11 leads into the township, the Garden State Parkway passes exits 127 through 132, and U.S. 1 and 9 share a corridor with Routes 27, 35, 184 and 440. NJ Transit stops at Metropark, Avenel and Woodbridge stations, and Metropark adds Amtrak. Woodbridge Center is the fourth-largest mall in New Jersey, and Wakefern Food Corporation, owner of ShopRite, has headquarters in Keasbey.

Water shapes many lots. Nearly one fifth of the land is inside FEMA flood hazard areas, with repeated tidal flooding along the Woodbridge River, the Raritan at Keasbey and the Arthur Kill at Sewaren and Port Reading. Schools belong to the Woodbridge Township School District, which operated 25 schools for 13,836 students in 2022 to 2023.

In Census estimates for 2020 to 2024, an owned home has a median value of $433,000, and renters pay a median $1,959 in gross rent. Households number 36,781 at 2.75 people each, and 40.6 percent of adults 25 and older hold a bachelor's degree. Two of every three homes are owner occupied, median household income is $108,928, and the average commute takes 32.5 minutes.

sections.h2: How big are the Woodbridge communities, and what green space do they share?
sections.html:
The 2020 census counted these places inside the township: Iselin 20,088, Woodbridge proper 19,839, Colonia 18,609, Avenel 16,290, Fords 12,941, Port Reading 3,921, Keasbey 3,027, Sewaren 2,885, Menlo Park Terrace 2,806 and Hopelawn 2,603.

Woodbridge keeps a lot of open ground for a place this dense. Merrill Park covers 179 acres along the South Branch Rahway River, the Oros Wildlife Preserve holds 67 acres on the Woodbridge River, and Heards Brook Park sits in the middle of Woodbridge proper. The Middlesex Greenway is a 3.5-mile rail trail from Metuchen to Woodbridge that forms part of the East Coast Greenway.

The township maintains 244.16 of its 303.32 miles of roads. The county looks after 28.79 miles, the state 17.69 and the Turnpike Authority 12.68, based on the 2010 road survey cited for the township.

sections.h2: What landmarks and history give Woodbridge its character?
sections.html:
Woodbridge claims the first gristmill in New Jersey, built by Jonathan Singletary Dunham, whose 1709 house still stands. In 1751 James Parker founded the first printing press in the colony here, and the restored building with a working press is in Parker Press Park, which hosts summer concerts. The township's motto is "The Best Town Around."

The Woodbridge Cloverleaf opened in 1929 where Route 25, now U.S. 1 and 9, met Route 4, now Route 35, and it was the first cloverleaf interchange in the world. A separate mark is the Governor Alfred E. Driscoll Bridge on the Garden State Parkway over the Raritan River, with 15 travel lanes among the widest and busiest bridges anywhere.

Parts of the township later became separate places: Rahway in 1858, Raritan Township, now Edison, in 1870, and Roosevelt, now Carteret, in 1906. A 1951 commuter train derailment that killed 85 people is remembered with two historical markers.

faqs.q: When do Woodbridge property taxes come due?
faqs.a: Installments are due February 1, May 1, August 1 and November 1. Bills go out in January and July.

faqs.q: Where can I pay a Woodbridge tax bill in person?
faqs.a: Use the Tax Collection Office on the first floor of Town Hall. Cash, checks and money orders are accepted, and the counter runs late on Tuesdays.

faqs.q: What does it cost to pay a Woodbridge bill online?
faqs.a: An electronic check costs $1.95. A credit or debit card costs roughly 2.95 percent of the payment.

faqs.q: Which body decides a Woodbridge assessment appeal?
faqs.a: The Middlesex County Board of Taxation decides it. Use the board's online portal, or call 732-745-3350 for guidance.

faqs.q: Does Woodbridge have a senior tax deduction?
faqs.a: Yes, a $250 annual deduction for qualifying owners 65 or older or disabled. File Form PTD to start it and Form PD5 by March 1 each year to keep it.
